1:
Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets the scene before the machinery: Canaan was not conquered to be left desert, and Israel, hitherto closely encamped in one body, must now disperse to replenish the new conquests. He appeals to Isaiah 45:18 — the earth was formed to be inhabited. Yet no man might settle where he pleased.

Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) explains why the three named parties stand in the order they do: Eleazar first, as the minister of God in sacred things; Joshua next, as holding supreme command in things civil; the heads of the fathers last, since in all things they acted under Joshua. He counts the princes as twelve with Joshua and Eleazar included, and notes that none was taken from Reuben or Gad, whose portion already lay beyond Jordan. Henry counts differently — ten princes, one from each tribe still to be provided for, so that every tribe might see fair dealing done. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds that Eleazar best understood the laws by which the division was to be regulated, and that where any of the men named at Numbers 34:17 had since died, others were put in their stead.

Why a lot at all, when the portions had already been indicated? Gill (reformed) gives three reasons: to forestall quarrels among the tribes, to display the agreement between the lot and the predictions of Jacob and Moses, and to make plain that the division was no private settlement of the men who administered it but the providence of God. Wesley borrows a learned man’s verdict that he must be more stupid than stupidity who does not acknowledge a divine hand here. Clarke observes that each tribe was found placed exactly where the dying Jacob and Moses had foretold — vineyards for Judah, seacoasts for Zebulun and Issachar, oil and metals for Asher, and for Benjamin a place all but between the shoulders of the temple.

Calvin (reformed) raises the hard question the narrative creates. If the land was divided by Joshua, Eleazar and the princes, how was it divided by lot, since a lot answers to no man’s will? To say that the men merely watched for fraud does not settle it. His answer is that they were appointed for a second task after the lot: to enlarge or restrict each tribe’s boundaries by the thousands the census had found in it. The lot alone set the districts, Judah at the head and Zebulun away to the seashore. Wesley reaches the same distinction in a sentence: the lot determined the parts but did not fix all the bounds. Calvin adds that the ten were named by the voice of God and not by the suffrages of men, so that suspicion of them would have been impious.

The arithmetic occupies the grammarians. Keil (grammatical-historical) works it: two tribes and a half settled beyond Jordan and Levi excluded appears to leave eight and a half, yet nine and a half were provided for, because Joseph’s sons became two tribes by Jacob’s adoption at Genesis 48:5; and the Levites, though landless, received towns with pasture surrendered out of the others’ inheritance. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same total and finds it embodied in the high priest’s dress at Exodus 28, where the shoulder-stones name Jacob’s sons by birth and the breastplate names the twelve tribes — two reckonings, each yielding twelve, both needed if the complete Israel was to be represented. Calvin observes that the Levites’ exclusion is now stated a third time, and reads it as God taking them to himself as his own peculiar inheritance. Clarke closes on the ground: the work began at Gilgal and was finished only at Shiloh. Gill lifts it at the last — Canaan is a type of the heavenly inheritance, which the saints obtain by lot in and through the antitypical Joshua.
6:
Caleb’s suit interrupts the survey, and Calvin (reformed) explains why: what he asks cannot wait on the lot. He asks in the heat of warfare, not for a district already cleared but for leave to win one by routing its giants — seeking only that when his valour has done the work he not be defrauded of its reward, which is why the mountain must stay out of the common lot. Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes it a principle: a lot appeals to God in cases that cannot otherwise be decided, not in those he has already determined.

Gill (reformed) reads the children of Judah as not the whole tribe but its chief men, come with their prince for his honour and to second his petition; Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds that they meant to testify their consent, so that none should take the grant as a reflection on the rest. Calvin sees a shrewder interest too: so extraordinary a benefit to one family was an addition to all. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) meets the suspicion that stepping forward first savours of self-interest: what Caleb asked was the most dangerous ground in his tribe’s inheritance, held by the gigantic sons of Anak. Of the two faithful spies he took his portion first and Joshua last of all Israel at Joshua 19:49 — the one foremost in a service of danger, the other last to seek his own.

The title Kenezite puzzles everyone and is settled by no one. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) thinks Kenaz more probably the father of Jephunneh, and Caleb named for him because it ran in the house, Othniel his son-in-law being called a son of Kenaz. Wesley says simply, of the posterity of Kenaz. Henry floats a title won by victory over the Kenezites, as the Romans named generals from the countries they conquered. Calvin declines to guess.

Caleb’s ground is his report and the oath it earned. Gill notes that he was one of twelve, one to a tribe, their ages given to show they were in the prime of their days for what the errand asked of them. On bringing back word as it was in his heart the witnesses converge: Clarke says neither fear nor favour influenced him, Wesley that he spoke sincerely when the others were biased by dread of the people. Calvin takes the heart as set against deceitful words, dismisses as a ridiculous fiction the notion that Caleb said it only inwardly for fear of his companions, and gives the next clause literally — I fulfilled to go after thy God. Keil (grammatical-historical) fixes my brethren as the other spies, Joshua excepted, since it is Joshua he addresses.

Does the self-praise sit well? Calvin admits it sounds loftier than becomes a modest man, and answers that so invidious a request needed commendation to suppress envy. Henry and Wesley reply otherwise: the testimony was God’s own first, given at Numbers 14:24, so repeating it is no more vain-glory than telling others what God has done for one’s soul.

The oath itself is the chapter’s textual crux. Clarke observes that where Caleb seems to point there is no word of any promise of Hebron, nor at Deuteronomy 1:36; he still thinks the trodden ground means Hebron. Ellicott will not go so far: whether Moses referred to Hebron specifically, it is impossible to say. Keil concludes that the recorded oath cannot be this one, since it promises Canaan at large and not Hebron, so a special promise must have been given and left unwritten. Ellicott mines the speech for the only direct evidence of the war’s length: Caleb was seventy-eight at the crossing and eighty-five at the division, so the conquest ran seven years. Calvin, counting otherwise, calls it the fifth year since they entered the land.
10:
Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) breaks the forty-five years up: thirty-eight in the wilderness and seven since they came into Canaan. Henry (puritan-evangelical) counts the same stretches by their dangers, and turns the sum on the reader: the longer we live, the more sensible we should be of God’s patience in prolonging forfeited lives. Gill (reformed) keeps it to the promise, which was that this man should see and possess the land, and so required health as much as life. Calvin (reformed) asks what the long life was for, and answers: the inheritance denied to all that generation.

The strength is the harder claim. Calvin notes that a green old age has fallen to others, but rarely with vigour unimpaired at eighty-five; Caleb claims not a leader’s skill only but a soldier’s strength, and to go out and to come in is Hebrew for discharging every part of one’s duty. Gill hears the same double claim, mind as sound as ever and body as hale, when so many thousands had fallen in the wilderness. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) gives it a voice: not a place to sit down in and take his ease, but a fight he is as able and willing for as forty-five years ago. Wesley adds that the strength claimed is for action, not counsel, and sets it against Psalms 90:10, that at eighty our strength is labour and sorrow; Caleb’s at eighty-five was ease and joy, got by following the LORD fully. Henry says the promise was outdone, since God gives more than he promises. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notices the comparison the chapter invites: Joshua had aged by Joshua 13:1, yet died at a hundred and ten, only twenty-five years Caleb’s senior. The weight of command, and perhaps temperament, may account for it.

What is asked for is a region, not a town. Gill reads this mountain as the hill country of Judea in which Hebron and Debir stood; Keil (grammatical-historical) fixes it from the context as the highland about Hebron where the spies met the Anakim at Numbers 13:22, and reads the two clauses of the request as co-ordinate rather than one subordinate to the other. Wesley explains the wording: Caleb names the country and not the cities, the cities being destined for the Levites at Joshua 21:11. Clarke raises the difficulty that Hebron had already fallen to Joshua, and concludes that the request must take in the surrounding country where the Anakim were still in force; he reports the conjecture that Hebron was retaken while the army campaigned elsewhere, and prefers the simpler reading.

Everything turns on the conditional. Wesley calls it modest and pious — owning both the necessity of God’s help and a godly fear lest his own sins forfeit it. Henry reads the hesitation as humility, not distrust: Caleb had said flatly that the LORD was with Israel, and speaks warily only of himself, resting on God’s presence and not on his valour, his tribe, or Joshua’s help. Calvin will not have it as doubt at all. Those who make it self-distrust say something to the point but not the whole; the word looks outward, at what men would think seeing the case. Israel trembled at the very name of the giants, and by setting the difficulty out plainly Caleb made his petition easier to grant: the princes conceded nothing but a perilous contest. His own mind shows in the next clause, that he shall drive them out as the LORD said; and how hard the work was may be judged from Joshua being dead before Caleb attempted it. Henry closes on the request: Caleb valued a promise above a providence, and chose ground the enemy held so that his brethren might be quickened to the like attempts — answering to his name, which signifies all heart.
13:
Joshua blessed him, and the witnesses ask what that was. Keil (grammatical-historical) takes it as imploring God’s blessing on the undertaking; Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) points out that to bless often means simply to speak well of a man, so it may cover praise for Caleb’s intrepidity as much as prayer that the LORD be with him. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps to the prayer; Gill (reformed) folds both together, a granting of the request and a wish for success against the giants. Calvin (reformed) reads the earnestness as deliberate: it was expedient to extol a valour that might incite others to surmount their fears, so that the praise works as an exhortation.

Clarke notes what the transaction settled: a full conveyance of Hebron and its dependencies to Caleb and his posterity, made before all the elders, so that the right stood outside the general determination by lot. Keil observes that Hebron is named as the chief city of the surrounding country, the highland Caleb asked for taking in the fortified town of Debir. Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks that the settlement was on Caleb and his heirs, for the reason the text itself gives.

Calvin raises a legal difficulty nobody else touches. Hebron became a Levitical city and a city of refuge: how could the grant hold? To say Caleb resigned his right will not do, since he is distinctly named the owner. His first answer is that what the Levites received was a right of dwelling, which leaves no inconsistency and leaves Caleb the credit of not refusing them hospitality in a place made his own. He then turns on his own solution: at Joshua 20:7 and Joshua 21:9 their title looks as complete as to any other city, and since those cities fell by lot, no wrong was done to Caleb — who, on all we know of him, would not have objected.

The old name draws the most comment. Gill sets out the possibilities without choosing: Kirjath-arba may be the city of the four, from four couples buried near it, from four eminent men who lived there, or from Anak and his three sons; or Arba may be a great man to whom the city belonged. He also reports a tradition that Hebron was named from a descendant of Caleb, making the present name an anticipation. Clarke prefers four Anakim, probably brothers, who built or conquered it, finding support in Caleb’s later expulsion of Anak’s three sons; but he concedes that Joshua 15:13 makes Arba a proper name, and derives Hebron from a root meaning to associate, fitting a seat of confederate chiefs. Wesley reads the great man as great in stature, strength and authority. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) is firmer: Arba was a man’s name. On which name is older he is careful — unless the Anakim are as ancient as the giant peoples of Genesis, Hebron must have been Hebron first, and yet Genesis 23:2 gives Kirjath-arba as the name of the place at Sarah’s death. Keil answers from the writer’s standpoint: before and unto this day belong to the time of composition, when Kirjath-arba had long fallen out of use, so nothing follows about which name came first. On one point two converge: Calvin refutes the notion that the city of four means the burial place of four patriarchs, which Clarke calls a self-confuting tradition.

The chapter ends where the wars ended. Clarke reads the last clause as the end of general campaigns: the Canaanites could make no further head together, each tribe being left to expel what remained in its own territory. Keil takes the repetition from Joshua 11:23 as a note that the distribution was not held up by the Anakim still in Hebron. Ellicott finds the clause natural in its earlier place, closing the record of the wars, and less easily accounted for here.
